\section{Results}\label{sec:5}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{5}

Every table in this section is taken directly from the authoritative, validated output files listed in Appendix A; no coefficient was computed for this chapter. Coefficients are reported with 95\% confidence intervals, except Table 5.4 (coefficients and p-values only). P-values are shown to three decimal places when at least .0005, and as ``\textless.001'' otherwise; full precision is stored in the authoritative files. Where a model has two inference conventions, both are labelled (Section 4.5), and prose uses the primary convention unless the sensitivity is named.

Household water and sanitation are entered together in every model (Sections 4.1, 4.2). No household coefficient reaches significance at the 5\% level in the cluster-fixed-effects specification, this thesis's main household result and the one least exposed to cluster-level confounding; water--HAZ crosses the 10\% threshold. Non-significance is read as inconclusive, not as proof no association exists. Under the more conservative FULL\_DUMMY\_DF sensitivity, the cluster-FE p-values widen to .080 (water--HAZ) and .574 (sanitation--HAZ) --- the same conclusion, using the normal reference distribution the baseline pipeline computes (Section 4.5), not the Student \emph{t}(\emph{G}−1) distribution used for the historical extension.

Slightly larger than Table 5.1/5.3's 36,040-child sample, since this specification does not require household WASH to be classifiable. The community coefficients, entered together at every stage, are large and highly significant before adjustment, attenuating sharply as controls are added; neither is significant fully adjusted. This pattern is consistent with confounding by local socioeconomic conditions, but does not, alone, establish it as the sole explanation --- a change in measurement structure as controls absorb variance could produce the same pattern. The same four-stage pattern holds for WAZ and WHZ, except WHZ's water association is already small and insignificant before adjustment (0.033, \emph{p} = .545). Across all three outcomes, the fully adjusted specifications (here and Table 5.1) show no consistent WASH--outcome association --- inconclusive evidence, not proof WASH has no true relationship with child growth.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{\ThesisRoot/figures/figure2_model4_coefficient_forest.png}
\ThesisFigureCaption{5.1}{Fully adjusted community water and sanitation coefficients (Table 5.2's final stage), pooled and by country, with 95\% confidence intervals.}
\end{figure}

Figure 5.1 breaks the fully adjusted stage out by country, for the same model, not a separate adjustment path. Of 30 country--outcome--exposure cells, one reaches significance at 5\%: Nigeria's community sanitation--HAZ coefficient (−0.184, \emph{p} = .035), already in Table 5.4. Several non-significant cells have comparable or larger point estimates --- Ethiopia's sanitation coefficients for WAZ (0.186) and WHZ (0.187) exceed Nigeria's in magnitude --- but wider confidence intervals that include zero, consistent with Ethiopia's smaller country subsample; their non-significance reflects imprecision, not a smaller true association, and the pooled null in Table 5.2 should not be read as averaging a uniformly small set of country effects.

One cell reaches significance at 5\%: household water for HAZ, conditional on the other three terms (β = −0.085, \emph{p} = .043), unexpectedly negative. Household and community water are correlated, and this is one significant cell among twelve in this table; it is reported as a single finding, not treated as central, and not read as evidence that improved household water is harmful.

The coefficient changes sign and grows in absolute size as controls are added sequentially. Removing wealth quintile alone from the full control set moves it from −0.457 back to −0.196, the largest movement from any single block --- sensitivity to specification, not proof wealth drives the reversal. The household-level coefficient for Nigeria is close to zero and not significant: the community-level, region-FE estimate is \textbf{not stable across specifications}, not evidence that improved sanitation harms growth in Nigeria. Appendix B.5 re-estimates the same fully adjusted community model under the binary WHO cutoffs, an alternative operationalisation of the same anthropometric measurements rather than an independent sample: it finds three, not one, nominally significant cells among 30, including Nigeria's sanitation--stunted coefficient in the same direction as here.

\subsection{Current-age heterogeneity}\label{sec:5.5}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.5}

Six current-age bands (0--5 to 48--59 completed months, 12--23 as reference) replace the continuous age control (Section 4.4). Of twelve exposure-specific joint interaction tests (two exposures × three outcomes × two fixed-effects structures, \(\chi^2\), 5 restrictions each), eleven of twelve reject no heterogeneity at 5\% (exception: water--WHZ under region FE, \emph{p} = .300); the combined ten-term tests reject in all six combinations (largest \emph{p} = .019). The household-WASH association with current outcomes therefore varies with current age in most specifications tested --- secondary evidence about the \emph{current} survey-date association only, which does not reconstruct any child's actual early-life exposure, the question the historical extension addresses under its own limitations.

\subsection{Historical extension: primary established-date models}\label{sec:5.6}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.6}

All cells come from the primary weighted models, post-12-month window, established-date sample (Ghana 2014, Kenya 2014, Nigeria 2018), per 10 percentage points of IHME-modelled local coverage --- an area average within each child's buffer, not a household record (Section 3.5). These are weighted conditional associations among eligible measured children, not population-representative, with confidence intervals and p-values from the Student \emph{t}(\emph{G}−1) distribution.

The pooled water--HAZ coefficient (1.03, \emph{p} \textless{} .001) is this section's selected headline. It is \textbf{not} the only nominally significant cell: six of 24 reach \emph{p} \textless{} .05 --- pooled water--HAZ, pooled water--WAZ, Ghana water--HAZ, Nigeria water--HAZ, Nigeria water--WAZ (\emph{p} = .0498) and Ghana sanitation--HAZ (negative). It was chosen as headline because it is the pooled estimate for this thesis's primary outcome and window, proposed in a dated specification document before any coefficient was estimated (Section 6.4), not because it is the only significant result. All 24 primary cells were independently reconstructed with a different estimation library on a separately rebuilt sample, matching stored values (Appendix B.2) --- confirming the specification, correctly implemented, produces these numbers, not a multiplicity correction and not evidence of causality.

\textbf{Weighted vs.~unweighted.} The pooled coefficient is sensitive to the equal-country weighting convention: 1.03 weighted versus 0.41 {[}0.03, 0.80{]}, \emph{p} = .035, unweighted on the identical 23,018 observations --- a disclosed sensitivity (Section 4.5), not evidence either weighting is more ``correct''; equal weight totals do not give equal influence on the pooled slope, which also depends on each country's residual exposure variation.

\textbf{Residual exposure variation.} The pooled model's residual within-cluster exposure standard deviation is 0.43 percentage points; the conventional 10-point coefficient scale is therefore approximately 23 times that standard deviation --- a scale benchmark, not a single identifying contrast or a bound on observed changes. One residual SD corresponds to approximately 0.044 HAZ standard deviations.

\begin{ThesisTableNote}

\emph{Note.} Per 10 percentage points, as Table 5.5. ``Own-eligible'' is each window's own sample; the common sample is eligible under all four.

\end{ThesisTableNote}

The first four rows each use their own window's eligible sample, so comparing them changes window and sample at once. The last row instead holds post-12-month fixed and changes only the sample, 1.03 to 1.64 --- a \textbf{sample-composition effect}, not evidence favouring one window's validity. The table gives no like-for-like comparison of all four windows on one sample. No window was selected for its coefficient's significance; all four were listed together in the same dated pre-estimation specification (Appendix C).

Adding wealth leaves the coefficient essentially unchanged, showing only that it is not sensitive to this adjustment; it neither establishes mediation nor adjudicates the competing confounding concern (Section 3.8), nor bears on cluster-fixed-effects absorption (Section 4.2). The spatial-method and completion-rule sensitivities move the coefficient by amounts smaller than, or comparable to, the weighted/unweighted gap; none is privileged over the main specification.

\subsection{Ethiopia: provisional, outside the established-date sample}\label{sec:5.9}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{5.9}

Ethiopia's three interview-date candidates are not equally valid. Candidate C1's 30-day Ethiopian-calendar arithmetic has already been shown invalid for the delivered date fields, independently of the WASH analysis (Appendix C); it is excluded from every reporting table. Candidates C2 and C3 remain provisional, neither independently validated; they agree closely (water--HAZ: −0.39 both; sanitation--HAZ: −0.45 both; all four confidence intervals include zero). These are reported only as an exploratory sensitivity, never pooled into or compared with the established-date headline results.
